Voids Vigil is a self titled "Brotato-lite" that I enjoy a great deal more than its inspiration. For those unfamiliar for that term this means that the player character automatically fires weapons to clear waves of enemies whilst scooting around the arena with a dash. After each wave, you can redeem in game currency to buy additional weapons, passive buffs, abilities that can be activated or drones to help you on the battlefield. It may sound like a lot to take in, but the tutorial is nice and even without it, I do think the gameplay and build are fairly intuitive (unlike its inspiration).  

The visuals are wonderfully crunchy pixel art and the soundtrack is fittingly intense and driving. There are multiple game modes including a campaign, a survival mode and a creative card battler. VV has a ton of unlockable classes each with their own twist. This game also has a deal of irreverence (as also seen in Caiysware's previous game, Boneraiser Minions); the character class of the Cog Sniffer did get me to roll my eyes.  The gameplay loop and minute to minute action is fantastic and a leader in the autobattler genre. 

If there was one thing that I would adjust, it would be to increase the visibility of my character and allies. There are options to toggle your color off the standard blue (which blends in with everything) but additional outlines or auras would help me suss out where I am on the map on higher difficulties amidst swarms of enemies and waves of fireballs. As it is, it is not bad, but I think it could be better. 

After my first six or so hours, I have had a great time with Voids Vigil and look forward to many hours to come. If you appreciate autobattlers but felt like Brotato was a bit too unforgiving, roll the dice on this one- you won't regret it.

There are things I enjoy about this game, it's fast paced, bite sized gameplay which you can play in-between short breaks. The pixel art is pretty good, the enemy variation is humongous, the music isn't bad either but it gets repetitive. 

There's a ton of characters, weapons, drones, abilities, upgrades, and achievements to unlock which feel quite satisfying. You have plenty of game modes, daily/weekly challenges, and even a Final Fantasy 8/9 style card game.

What doesn't work in my opinion is that the game  is overly chaotic, overwhelming, and cluttered. There's a ton of text and information popping up on the screen at once, the overly juvenile equipment information makes it harder to parse and detracts from the overall experience (especially if you're not a native English speaker).

Boneraiser minions did the "Vampire Survivor" style gameplay better, it was also more organized and packed into a neat package. You always knew what all your minions did, what you had to do to upgrade them, and how to progress with unlocking new content. Here on the other hand you just roll with it and figure it out as you stumble along, it honestly doesn't feel as satisfying as it could've been.

I enjoy this game even with its faults, I certainly enjoy it far more than Vampire Survivors but it's not nearly as good as Boneraiser Minions. It just needs to better explain what you're doing, what you're progressing towards, and how to combine your upgrades into better upgrades.

One thing is for sure, caiys is a beast at responding to community issues, fixing bugs, adding accessibility settings, as well as post-release content. They should be highly praised for that.

Unfortunately I have to painstakingly rewrite my whole review as my opinion on the game has changed drastically, I no longer think it's "good" but might actually be the second coming of Jesus. Let me explain.

----------

Voids Vigil, like Caiys other games, have waaay too much content. There are four different game modes including a card game. The amount of stuff for a really cheap early access game is appreciated but it's still not the reason I enjoy Void's Vigil so much.

I have touched NONE of the gamemodes other than Rogue Convergence, but that mode alone manages to single-handedly solve almost every problem the "Survivors/Brotato-like" genre has.

(Voids Vigil will be refered to as VV henceforth, I will only be discussing the Rogue Convergence gamemode)

----------

VV starts out somewhat hectic, there's not *that* much happening, but more compared to it's contemporaries. The dev has outright stated that this is the intention, when compared to his other game Boneraiser Minions which has a larger focus on meta-progression. While there IS meta-progression it's almost entirely horizontal, offering new challenges and things to try out but not a vertical power increase.

One of VV's trump cards is the insane escalation that occurs during a run, and especially subsequent difficulties. The game gets HECTIC, this makes it incredibly engaging. In something like Vampire Survivor's it can sometimes feel like you are "waiting" the last 10-15minutes to see if your build can make it, but in VV the next choice is always close-by and interesting.

VV works with a shop system similar to Brotato where you buy upgrades between "rounds" of gameplay. Where VV is a straight up improvement on the former (sorry Brotato I love you) is in how great the shop system is. What shops you get are entirely randomised, and may include sales, shady merchants selling you temporary bonuses, or scoundrels demanding a payment for not giving you a negative effect if you visited the wrong guy.

----------

Here are some more direct examples of how VV solves problems of the genre:

1. Interesting choices during rounds. Rounds/levels are not just places to test out your build but to make choices that will impact the whole run. Do you keep the spawners alive for more enemies but more reward? Do you let a jammer extend the length of the Sector but risk being overwhelmed in the last seconds?

2. VV's difficulties directly impact how long a run is and the amount of items in the pool. This means a run is simultaneously lean/compact compared to contemporaries but still allows for longer sessions at higher difficulties.

3. Actual gameplay. The game features both active skills and a dodge which actually matters. These are your ways to manage the challenges you take on in search for bigger rewards.

4. Score-play is alive. Scoring is a way to play games which have kinda fizzled out in recent years, but it's a great way to contextualize gameplay mechanics. Of course it's optional, but players who want to chase score have the option to do so by picking upgrades which increase score gain while reducing things like max health.

With all these things combined the game manages to never be boring for even a second.

----------

Below are some of critiques, but they are few and far between.

- I find the game quite dark, I also had this problem with Boneraiser but that was fixed with accessibility options. I did not find the same options here unfortunately, but I might just have missed them.

- As the game is actually somewhat difficult and hectic, I feel a visual hitbox indication might be needed. It's also quite zoomed in, which makes dodging feel a bit cluncky, especially when most bosses attack you horizontally and the player is noodle shaped (you'll get what I mean when you play it).

While this obviously adds to the hectic feeling of the game, some of the bosses are actually kinda though to dodge! I feel like a visual hitbox indication (like Touhou or other shmups) and a sliiiight zoom out would go a long way.

If projectile size needs to be larger to compensate for the difficulty then I think it's still a good tradeoff.

There are two currently available game modes, Rogue Convergence and Survival Function.

Rogue Convergence plays with a Brotato-like structure, where you survive for rounds, collect money, and then spend the money in shops between rounds. I *really* like Rogue Convergence. I think the balance is mostly great, and while I thought it was easy at first, the higher difficulties are a really satisfying experience. Money is scarce enough that you have to make real choices, and you're rewarded for thinking ahead and responding cleverly to current shops.

My only real criticism of Rogue Convergence is that it doesn't have an unlimited mode as far as I can tell, and that's a shame -- this is really the game mode that I want to play forever.

Survival Function plays more like Vampire Survivors, where collecting "money" simply spawns a chest that you get choices of loot from, and you play endlessly and collect as much loot as you can. This mode appears to be infinite, but I think it's really much less fun. The game is challenging, and having less control -- all in the form of shop rerolls -- is a lot less interesting than the higher control but tighter budget offered in Rogue Convergence.

Overall, there *are* some balance issues I think:

Schematics are absurdly strong, especially in Rogue Convergence. They apply to all of your weapons, and you can stack as many of them as you want, so good weapons pales in comparison to the importance of lots of schematics. They also don't seem particularly balanced -- it's very difficult to find sources of crit, but the sources that exist give you +25% and +50% crit chance to all guns (one is a Device, one is a Schematic), making them simultaneously completely absurd while making other things, like increased crit damage, totally useless unless you stumble upon those items.

Some of the weapons also feel much much stronger than others, but I may just have more learning to do. Weapons like the bubble launcher and combination weapons like the black hole launcher and the BFG feel like they completely outclass other weapons once you have Stable blueprint (which causes their giant, slow-moving projectiles to also last forever).

I think that clarity is a problem both visually and information-wise. While some of the fun of the game comes from the fact that some of the mechanics are not directly explained and you need to discover them a little bit on your own, this "fun" will evaporate when people write guides for the game, so I wish things like projectile interactions and more detailed weapon stats were accessible in game (e.g. attacks per second).

Visually, while the game is stylish as hell and I think it looks great, when things get too cluttered all clarity is lost. While you always die in games like this to being overwhelmed by enemies, I die earlier than I would in e.g.  Brotato because I simply can't tell what the hell is going on. This is, of course, something I'll get better at over time, but I do feel like the incredibly low-resolution pixel art might be partially to blame.

The dash mechanic is really great though, I think my favorite such implementation. Making it a meter that you spend for arbitrary lengths of time gets rid of the issue in e.g. Tiny Rogues where fixed distance dashes make going over some projectiles safely super difficult, while also allowing super fine-grained resource management. I think I can still get a lot better at it, not the easiest version for me to wrap my head around. It's super OP and I think I'm underusing it.

BM is arguably better than Vampire Survivors(in my humble opinion) and even if you ere on the side of the original BM is an easy top 3 or 5 in the genre. Voids Vigil is another strong entry, having more in common with Brotato. Any way you slice it caiys has two strong bullet heavens for a great price... and you can go play VS and Brotato alongside these two gems as well, all for less than $20 total! What a steal! All these games stand shoulder to shoulder and VV has come along during the solemn wait for the Brotato expansion as a very welcome surprise.

Voids Vigil is a touch story light, carrying itself on strong aesthetics and fast, frantic arcadey gameplay first and foremost. Strange automated space stations staffed by killer robots orbit a spooky void in space, you are tasked by equally spooky robot taskmasters to pilot a lil' vessel guy through the sectors, destroy the boss and submit your experiences to the AI hivemind for convergence! Something like that... clear the stages, enjoy the fun build experimentation, place high scores.

VV starts simply, as these games tend to. You pick a weird lil' guy, some benefits, some drawbacks, and a weapon. Pick up goodies, kill as many enemies as you can without dying, go to shops to steadily improve. These games favor automatic fighting but there is an invulnerable dash button necessary for evading danger, with room to expand the energy pool it draws from but always emptying quickly, providing a high skill ceiling for the best timings. With a wide pool of options you're drawn to make as many pleasing synergies as possible to stay ahead of the rising stage difficulty. The more you can kill the more loot you can get so that you can kill more, repeating. Discovering synergies is intuitive and pleasing, though VV goes for elevating your decision making with things like the elements systems. Important to all classes, with the first few pushing the importance of building a strong singular element for reliable guns(though not mandatory), stats are roughly divided into body, element and loadout(gun, droid, ability slots.) If you're holding brown(argon) guns and stack argon element you deal more damage, you can get a passive stat booster that adds your argon element stat to your body(hp, energy, speed, defense, recovery) and makes you more survivable and so on. You can build for crossover between elements and there are several neutralish classes, as well as early difficulties limiting the available elements.

From there you can fill out 5+ gun slots, 5+ drone slots(automatic helpers) and 2+ ability slots, activated or automatic boosts like the spells of Boneraiser. Some classes emphasize different approaches or aspects of the system and there's a great dance between pushing a strength as high as it can go while still maintaining some balance. Having 8 strong drones won't save you from a stray hit if you have no boosts to body stats! But maybe if you blow everything away with brute force it won't matter... there's also a clever system where each individual gun has a strong trait, like setting enemies on fire or homing shots. For each gun you hold you can extract that trait as a blueprint you copy and paste to every other gun you have. If you go for 5 of the same strong gun you miss out on 4 free traits and so on, though you can buy them directly from the shop, the free blueprint copy is a bonus for diversifying your loadout. Likewise you can pour resources into say abilities, eventually making them passive autocast and reopening your slots to pick up more, which you can also work to making passive autocast, repeating! Much like Boneraiser, VV works to elevate gameplay with a spread of systems and decisions beyond the auto-battling near-idler roots of the genre.

My favorite part of the balance of VV is the tug of war between survival and score. You can disable enemy spawners to make a level safer or leave them up to get more loot, kills and points. You can buy items to make yourself stronger or invite even more danger in. Doing both is ideal, the best score-chasers make things as dangerous as possible while staying alive! VV features a great survival mode that streamlines the entire stage by stage convergence process, letting you quickly experiment with and push builds and brutally punishing efforts to stay alive once the harder kill waves enter while you shoot for going for high score on the leaderboards. There's the traditional caiys cute card game as an extra and although it is not present yet in early access there will be a more developed convergence campaign mode with stage selection.

If VV is anything like Boneraiser's EA journey I am quite excited as BM ended up being about 400-500% bigger than the first form of the completed game! VV is already a full title that can easily eat 5-10 hours in seeking full completion, even more if you push for high scores and satisfying your build curiosity. I won't say VV is in a perfect state yet, there's room for adjustments to class balance and so on, but caiys has already delivered several times over. Play VV, it is worth $10 easily and you get it for $3 or less. Then play Brotato, Boneraiser and so on(Skelly Selest is good too!) If you like one of these games you're certain to like the others. The ironclad loop of experimentation to go further makes these games that may seem small at first glance into addictive little titans of gameplay.

Feels guilty paying only $2.39 for this amount of effort, like all games from Anthony it should probably be a $10 release even in the early access, but what I can I say, dev is so generous, even some purchases in the game seem to give the currency back. I said plenty of complements about the dev over the years, so I won't drill on that too much, in my opinion some of the better rogue-lites you can buy for content and vibes, as well as just supporting his games and listening to feedback probably better than any other developer I met. Even when you complain, he somehow makes it into game features, if you follow the dev long enough, you know the history about the legendary Diaper. 

Like his previous game it's somewhat inspired by the Vampire Survivors, but to a lesser extent, instead of having generic level up system, you get a random assortment of shops between each floor that sell active weapons, passives, and various cooldown trinkets, many of which can be upgraded into more powerful versions. I didn't think I would like the system at first because it kinda feels like you are a bit lost, but once the difficulty ramps up it's more fun to plan and navigate your way by resource management, taking risk with certain items, and eventually finding the build you looking for. There is no way of aiming manually, it's automatic, not sure how I feel about that, personally I would prefer having both, but it still works well enough.

The game is still missing one important mode, but if you keep replaying the regular gauntlet on higher difficulty, you will find new content like new items, new bosses, and new levels, eventually unlocking a card game, and an endless mode which can be played in multiple difficulties. You could probably drop more than 5 hours into it before it starts to get a little repetitive, but it kinda depends if you enjoy the difficulty enough, personally I do think it gets a bit too cluttered for my taste, but for the price it's still a fantastic purchase, even though I think I prefer your previous releases for gameplay.

I did run into some crashes mainly with the minion builds, that said I am not too worried, like I said, Case has a history of fixing his game very fast, if anything some issues are expected on the release day, perfectly normal. Other than that I don't have too many complaints other than a few minor balancing issues, it does get kinda hard to see once you get a build going, but I guess it's part of the genre at this point, no way around it.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

(+) A lot of replay value for low price, you can grind a couple of modes already, pretty much until you get bored really, you can unlock more characters, more weapons, different modes, and so on. Similar to his previous games, it has the card game, endless, map mode (not out yet), and the regular floor mode.

(+) Always enjoyed your slightly dark pixel art, you really love purple don't you. Aside from looking good, I think killing things feels very satisfactory, nice pop sounds. Good music, even though it's not made for the game, works with the game really well.

(+) Has a decent amount of complexity and challenge to it, and I find that builds are very flexible, you can get away doing all kinds of things as regular enemies don't get too tanky. Good risk vs reward elements, many items that reward you for increasing enemy count and such.

[h1] Feedback: [/h1]

- still crashes with some builds for a number of people, but I mean it's the first day so it's expected, Case pretty active usually so I am not too concerned.

- personally I would prefer if you color coded the stores, I know there is an icon, but I feel it would be easier to remember what you looking for, maybe weapons red, passives blue, gems orange, and so on.

- it's a bit weird that the first mode you unlock is the one in development, might confuse people (keep replaying on higher difficulty, you will unlock more things)

- I would consider maybe having more items that can prevent burst damage, or maybe a mechanic that would prevent you from getting instantly killed. I know there is a potion that does so, but it just feels lame whenever you die too fast when dashing into a crowd. You could even have a base mechanic that always triggers on last hit point, just so you at least get 2 chances to dodge a crowd (once per stage maybe)

Voids Vigil is a Brotato-like. I'm not even a fan of Brotato, nor am I much of a fan of its clones/games inspired by it. So why am I giving this game a positive review you ask?

The answer is: it's by far way, way better than the original Brotato in my opinion. No, i'm serious when I say that. Although in this game, the weapons are always auto firing, that doesn't mean it's too simple since the element affinity aspect, many passive/active items, and other things, all give it some extra depth. And on the other hand it's not too absurdly difficult, the difficulty feels just right...at least until you hit the survival mode and it turns really hard, but I don't even mind that. Because Voids Vigil is, unlike Brotato, actually FUN in my very honest opinion.

In fact, I believe this is the developer's best game yet. I've played Boneraiser Minions and although that game was fun enough, this one is even better. Sure, there are a handful of weird/dirty jokes, (a diaper item, the number 69 appearing ad nauseam, etc.) but they do nothing to sink the game as a whole because, again, it's genuinely enjoyable. I actually think that all the quirks from the cool synthwave soundtrack to the many unlockables and score chasing gameplay and even the Sci-fi motif, everything adds to the experience. The result is that I believe Voids Vigil is the best Brotato-like I have ever seen and one that manages to be highly replayable, fun, and addicting. Also, runs are also neither too long or too short even if you decide to go in the endless survival mode given the game's quick and do-or-die nature.

I only wish that this game gets more attention. In this game, there doesn't seem to be as many players compared to Boneraiser Minions if the leaderboards and seeded challenge runs are anything to go by. But in conclusion, Voids Vigil is absolutely worth your money, despite its low price I totally recommend it and I think you'll find it to be a great experience.

If you love Vampire Survivors or Brotato, this game is from the same team that created Boneraiser Minions. Multiple difficulties and classes to unlock. I played 7 hours and barely scratched the surface of the game. Voids Vigil is a sci-fi robot roguelike. [/b]

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

- Multiple modes to try out- campaign mode, Rogue Convergence (Rogue mode where you navigate map similar to STS), Voidworld Trials (random daily runs), and even a high score mode with random classes.
- Each run will be different with diverse ways to choose your build- drones, abilities, and lures. Lures that will cause more enemies to spawn to get more cogs.  Cogs are the currency to buy items.
- Game mixes elements from Roguelike and space shooters. There is a stranger event that allows you to buy cogs for abilities/shop items or trade off health/stats for bonuses. Enemies come in waves from left and right side and there is a 60-80 second limit on the level to survive and collect cogs.

Below is an example of high score mode. It's great for challenging yourself and comparing your score to other players.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3518577513

[h2]Cons: [/h2]
- The high variety of weapons and RNG. There is RNG to get weapon shop upgrades and there are so 5 different elements, so buying items that buff a certain element may not synergize with all your weapons.
- Bosses are not as interesting compared to other Roguelike games. For the most part, they shoot projectiles at you and have multiple parts that you need to kill including the core. 

[b]Conclusion:
This is a unique game with good soundtrack and high replay ability. Some reviewers said if you played Boneraiser game, this is almost the same game. I did not play that one, so I don't have a previous Caiys game to compare it to. If you lose, you are compelled to start a new run and try a different build. You can easily reach 20-30 hours to unlock more achievements or if you want to beat the harder difficulties. [/b]

Also, and very strangely, the game is absolutely riddled with juvenile innuendo—so much so that it's actually distracting. If you're 13, maybe you'll find it funny, but, as an adult, I'm kind of just scratching my head. There's quite a bit of care taken to establish a sci-fi atmosphere, so it seems odd to throw it all away with constant 69 jokes and thinly-veiled puns that are bound to get caught in the Steam censor. I know Caiys games usually have a lightheartedness to them, but this one is weird. I loved bonerasier minions and I really enjoyed the first demo/alpha that was released for this game. However, I am very disappointed with the direction this game went in. Lots of systems exist in this game that are awkward or just unfun. 

Edit 1: I wasn't sure if this was confirmed until now, but apparently there is a soft cap on the amount of cogs you can get each level. Not only does this mean you HAVE to get cog items and enemy spawners just to reach nearly the same amount of cogs every level, but you get no fulfilling progress on your econ throughout the game. Feels like another underbaked, deeply unsatisfying mechanic.


- Most of the characters are either completely unfun (the first 5 characters are just copy and pasted versions of each other that promote you limiting your build as much as possible) or outright bad (cog gobbler is beyond bad and wretch, blacksmith, and merchant are all also bad)
- Each difficulty limits what weapons and elements you can use. Why is this an issue? Well, if you start with a weapon that isn't argon at the first difficulty of either campaign or endless (and you can start with any noncombination weapon in the game) you cannot upgrade that weapon AT ALL for the rest of the run. Not to mention, if you're playing one of the 5 copy and pasted characters who's a higher tier than the difficulty, you're flat out useless
- The element system is both boring, restricting, and very weird. All weapons have an element that they get increased stats with the more of said element you have. You can also get body stats from elements too (which are very important), but you have to hope you fish for an item that lets you get body stats from these elements in the first place. Not only is juggling different elements usually not worth it, but its entirely luck dependent on if you get the elements you want in the shop. Not to mention a solid portion of the elemental upgrades (like the temporary stat buffs or generators apart from endless) are useless or not worth the cogs. Apart from that, the elements do nothing on their own and have no flare that makes each element unique apart from them being associated with different stages and weapons. If you shuffled the elements around for each weapon, it would make zero difference in the game. 
- Your shop options can be taken up with locked items! This means that you can theoretically have only 1 choice in the shop, or none at all!
- Weapon traits are very spammy and promote very little strategy. Each weapon has a trait that makes it unique and can be applied to other weapons to combine effects (such as one weapon having explosive projectiles and another having homing shots). However, you have very little agency when it comes to acquiring these traits. If you want your weapons to have multiple traits, you have to buy them from a shop which applies the weapon traits to ALL of your weapons, even ones that don't have a use for certain traits. This means that you can't build each individual weapon you have to a certain style, its either all or nothing. Also, because having a weapon lets you have that perk for free in the shop (it might also have a higher chance to appear too, not sure?) this promotes you buying and selling weapons for as many perks as you can so you can just add as much text as possible to weapons, removing every inch of strategy for weapon choice. In the first alpha, weapon traits were passed on with a weapon combination system, where you could merge weapons together to get increased stats and a combo of traits. This system was FAR superior to the one we have now (apart from promoting you to only having 1 super weapon instead of multiple, I still believe the combination system with tweaks and limitations would be better than the one we have now)
- Speaking of weapon traits, correct me if I'm wrong but I'm pretty sure you just can't get them in endless mode at all apart from the default ones weapons come with
- Environments are more or less the same between each stage, apart from color background differences and new map nodes. Most enemies are recolored or re-skinned versions of each other with little variation in how you handle them, especially as you progress in difficulties
- This is super nitpicky, but the "Card game" the dev likes to add to their games in this version isn't nearly as fun as Bonerasier's game, but that might just be a me thing. It also seems much more difficult to win
- If anything I said here is subject to taste, the one thing I can say for certain is that the "final boss" of each difficulty is the least inspired and most boring boss I think I have ever faced in video gaming history. Each boss is just a recolored version of this idle, base thing that shoots at you, with each difficulty replacing an attack for a new one. Little to no variation at all

I really hope a lot of these issues gets improved, as the game has a really cool visual style and great soundtrack. I know the dev makes amazing stuff but this game just has not landed for me yet. It's a shame too, the unfinished campaign mode looks like it would be seriously fun, but its not out yet.

[u][b]Voids Vigil[/b][/u] is a very generic and average horde survival arena shooter which does nothing exceptional, nor adds anything new to the genre, to make it stand out from its competitors. Moreover, it is basically a clone of [u][url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1944570/Boneraiser_Minions/]Boneraiser Minions[/url][/u], the developer's previous game, except that you use weapons instead of letting minions fight for you, it has been reskinned to have a dark and dystopian sci-fi aesthetic, and it has a (slightly) more serious tone but is still chock full of sexual and raunchy innuendos which feel out of place.

Overall, I don't recommend it because it's a soulless copy of Boneraiser Minions that is riddled with bugs and the developer barely seems to playtest updates before releasing them, resulting in a painful Early Access that felt extremely amateurish and made it seem like they simply wanted funding throughout the Alpha and Beta stages of the game rather than developing a more complete product before release. Additionally, the juvenile potty humor which has unfortunately been carried over from Boneraiser Minions (where it fit much more naturally) doesn't fit this type of aesthetic nearly as well and has gotten stale, making the jokes feel out-of-place and overused.

Note: this review is current as of Patch v11.5 released on 14 March 2025 and will only be updated for major patches which add significant gameplay changes or achievements.

[quote][b]R E V I E W[/b][/quote]

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
The gameplay is typical for the horde survival genre and introduces nothing new to make the game even remotely unique or exciting. Although discovering things for the first time and learning the mechanics is initially thrilling, this exhilaration quickly wears off after a few hours as you will realistically have seen everything that the game has to offer despite its wide cast of classes, the multitude of weapons, and the plethora of abilities, drones, and passive items.

Although the classes each have slightly different mechanics, the majority of them aren't unique enough to truly give a different experience from one another which ultimately leads to runs feeling the same and only slightly changes how you approach the game from a tactical perspective.

The weapons also have a similar issue because there is no discernable difference between them and, thus, they feel superficial rather than impactful. Despite this, there is an interesting system which groups the weapons by, and scales their damage based on, certain elements but the game is easy enough that this system can be completely ignored by casual players; however, taking advantage of it makes the game extremely easy and you can easily delete bosses within a second of spawning into the arena. The only time that you might want to take advantage of this is if you are playing on the hardest difficulty (which still isn't that challenging) or if you are competing for a high score on the leaderboards.

The game has five different game modes:
- Story, where you go from arena to arena, visit shops in between each, and fight the boss at the end;
- Campaign, which is the same as the story mode except there is an open map and you can choose which nodes to visit;
- Survival, where you try to stay alive for as long as possible until the enemies outscale you or your computer can no longer run the game;
- Daily/weekly seeded runs, where you can compete in a challenge run for a high score on the leaderboard; and
- Card mini-game, which is similar to [i]Triple Triad[/i] from [u][url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/39150/FINAL_FANTASY_VIII/]Final Fantasy VIII[/url][/u] but is stripped-down and isn't worth playing at all.

The campaign mode was added with the full release of the game and completely dwarfs the story mode because it is much more immersive and engaging which results in the story mode feeling pointless in comparison. This begs the question of why didn't the game have the campaign mode from the start since it would have been a far superior foundation for the game and instead the developer spent the six months of Early Access adding an unnecessary amount of classes, weapons, and fixing an endless amount of bugs on a bi-weekly basis.

[h3]Graphics[/h3]
The graphics are made up of very colorful and retro-styled pixel art which looks quite good and unique in contrast to the purposely dark and gritty backgrounds.

[h3]Sound[/h3]
The soundtrack is composed of decent royalty-free dark and gritty synthwave songs which match the theme and aesthetic of the game quite well and don't become irritating despite looping quickly; however, they aren't worth listening to outside of the game unless you're really into the genre. The sound effects are amazing with a proper set of headphones as they are deep and resounding.

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story is vague and minimalistic, only being presented in cryptic messages shown prior to the title screen and whenever you win a run. The concept has plenty of potential for expansion, especially if it were to lean more into the hacker theme but I don't think anything else will be done with it despite the fact that the developer has the ability to write eloquently as evidenced by their quippy tutorial dialogue which made me laugh a few times.

[h3]Miscellaneous[/h3]
The in-game status menu is annoying to navigate because the icons of all passive items that you have collected are displayed on one panel at the bottom of the screen and, whenever you select one to see its details, its description box covers the entire panel and your passive items which is utterly baffling to me -- instead, they should have been split up into their own categories on a separate page since you can collect so many of them.

Another thing which is odd about the status menu is that it has a "Config" option where you can only change visibility options but no other game options such as audio, visual or controls; however, they are available via the pause menu which renders the Config option on the status menu completely redundant and this kind of design choice shows the lack of thought that the developer has put into the finer details of the game.

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
Overall, I don't recommend it because it's simply a very average, run-of-the-mill game and if you've already played Boneraiser Minions then you've essentially played this game as well because there is barely any functional difference between the two. My first few hours with it were somewhat fun but the achievements rapidly became a chore to keep up with and the Early Access has been quite unpleasant due to many missing features and game-breaking bugs.

Not actually a Brotatolike. Like, not even close. Play Brotato instead if you find this to be too fast and too projectile spammy with a bit too much RNG reliance for your tastes. (I have 100% achievements in Brotato on Epic, DLC included.)

This is actually closer to any bullet hell games you can think of, especially if they have explosions, close-range attacks, attacks from offscreen, lasting projectiles, long bursts of projectiles that can 3-hit you, and a need to constantly upgrade damage while also hoping and praying to get the projectile speed down relic or the trait that makes weapons shielding to make getting through viable...

...it goes deeper than that, though, EA was fine, good even... Then the Score-based hackables came in and threw off the Cog balancing, now you're more likely to see pointless score-increasing hackables than the infinitely more useful cog crates, which in the case of the fast-moving Haulers, are actually a THREAT to your run (you have to stay still and follow a tiny aoe in a game with bullets and enemies flying everywhere :/ ). Boneraiser had chests, sure, but those could also contain relics and spells, they had a use outside of gems for score- hell they even gave you gold to further the metaprogression and/or fund the Strangers who could appear in the run (until you got all the metaprog, then it does more or less just become "more score lol").

Against Brotato, cogs *dissapear* here, timebased and at end of zone, instead of being banked for the next zone like they are in Brotato... so you're getting around 140 - 220 cogs every zone. Surprised that I know the range? It's because that's how it's balanced... unlike Boneraiser, there's no good way to actually boost your material gain without seriously endagering yourself and your run through Lures - it worked in Boneraiser because you had a minion army who could attack at decent range with more than just 6 attacks, and if you picked those kinds of items and spells, it'd be because you were already somewhat above the needed curve and wanted to put yourself a bit above it, and in Brotato, it'd be because you were running enough Pierce, fast enough melee, or had explosions to compensate, here it's just a flat amount and that's it, everyone takes that one currency and everything costs 25 at the least, but there's 3-5 shops with 8ish options each and no real way to get more! Rerolling even costs more cogs if you're trying to stack one of those merchants specifically, with an unreasonable scale-up for every reroll every time you do it. Brotato only has 4 items in its shop, and factors locking and using some for rerolling into your usual, unaltered, generally-ok-run material amount.

With all that in mind.... There's no hit achievements and characters if you're even thinking "hey maybe I can still get 100% anyway". No. No you can't. Conservators and the other big boy from Campaign shoot SETS of homing bullets. Good luck if you still try now knowing that.
